description: NASA Space Apps 2024 Local Impact Winner and 2025 Global Nominee, with skills in GIS, satellite data, Earth observation, AI/ML, and NASA datasets. Building MOMAR, a Mars route-planning and planetary intelligence concept. Seeking teammates skilled in frontend/UI, 3D visualization, UX design, planetary science, data processing, or path planning to create an impactful lunar/Martian exploration solution.
summary:
MOMAR (Moon + Mars) is a web-based mission-planning platform designed to help future astronauts plan lower-risk, science-rich Marswalks. It integrates data from NASA's Mars orbiters and rovers, including HiRISE, CTX, CRISM, THEMIS, MOLA, Perseverance and Curiosity, into one interactive map.

Astronauts can explore Jezero Crater, Gale Crater and other locations across Mars, analyse terrain, compare the shortest and lower-risk routes, assess terrain hazards, and check whether the outbound and return journey fits the available EVA time budget. MOMAR also identifies potential scientific stops using mineral detections, geological features and rover observations, allowing crews to plan exploration and rehearse traverses in 3D.

We are also developing SOZO, an AI mission copilot and physics-based rover simulation environment to help interpret mission plans and evaluate robotic operations across different planetary conditions.

By bringing fragmented planetary data into one transparent, integrated planning environment, MOMAR aims to help explorers make better-informed decisions, reduce mission-planning risks and discover more during every Marswalk. The platform also extends to lunar south-pole exploration.
details:
What it does

MOMAR is a mission planner for walking on Mars. Before every Marswalk, an explorer has three questions, and MOMAR answers each one with real mission data.

  1. Where should I go? MOMAR stacks orbital imagery from 25 cm to 2.6 km per pixel with the USGS geologic map, CRISM mineral signals, THEMIS and TES thermal inertia, IAU feature names, and the actual traverses and photographs of Perseverance and Curiosity, all in one view.
  2. How do I get there safely? MOMAR turns terrain models into slope, roughness and a risk grid. It then plans two routes from A to B through up to eight stops: a shortest route and a lower-risk route. It uses any-angle Theta* search, with A* as a tested fallback. The two routes appear side by side (distance, walking time, steepest slope, share of steep ground), and the walk back to base is checked against an EVA time budget.
  3. What science can I do on the way? MOMAR flags stops where minerals appear, where the mapped geology changes, or where the ground turns to rock. Every stop shows its evidence and how confident MOMAR is.

It also includes:

  • A Mars clock (Mars24), the Sun’s position and terrain shadows, so you can see which parts of a route are sunlit at the planned time.
  • Archived surface weather from Perseverance’s MEDA instrument and climate data from MCS. These are always labelled as archived and never shown as live.
  • A full-screen 3D playback of the traverse, with the Perseverance rover and a walking astronaut.
  • A built-in Mission Scientist that works offline and answers questions using the plan’s own numbers, plus SOZO, an optional AI assistant.
  • A mission report and a GeoJSON export of both routes.
  • MOMAR Lunar, the same workflow at the Moon’s south pole on LOLA terrain. It uses Sun and Earth positions from JPL Horizons and temperatures from Diviner, and it plans routes for an Apollo LRV, a VIPER-class rover or an astronaut on foot.

How it works

A Python pipeline (rasterio/GDAL, NumPy, Shapely) pulls products from the planetary archives and reprojects them onto one shared grid per region. When a file is too large to download, the pipeline reads only the bytes it needs. One example is a 3.6 GB Gale terrain model. The output is compact tiles and JSON, plus a manifest that records the source of every layer. The web app (Next.js, React, TypeScript) draws the map with Leaflet and the globe and 3D playback with Three.js. Route planning runs in a Web Worker inside the browser, so the planner needs no server.

Why it can be trusted

  • Every layer has an info card showing its mission, instrument, resolution, date, licence and status: real, sampled, streamed, derived, illustrative or missing.
  • Assumptions are labelled as assumptions. The 25° slope limit, walking speed, 4-hour EVA budget and risk weights can all be edited, and all are marked “planning assumptions, not NASA suit or EVA limits”. MOMAR never calls a route “safe”. It only says “lower risk under these assumptions”.
  • The terrain is checked against real rover data.
    • At Gale, the terrain model matches Curiosity’s 1,386 recorded elevations with a median error of 0.0 m, and 90% fall within ±1.5 m.
    • At Jezero, in all three test scenarios, every point on Perseverance’s recorded drives lies on ground the planner treats as walkable.
  • Sun and Earth positions are cross-checked against NASA NAIF’s SPICE toolkit.
  • 516 automated tests cover routing, terrain, time, shadows and data handling.

Benefits and intended impact

Mission planners, scientists and students get one place to see what the data says about a site and how far each conclusion can be trusted. Before an EVA, a crew could compare routes and understand why one carries less risk, not just that it does. Because MOMAR separates what is measured from what is assumed, it also shows which new data would improve a plan the most, such as boulder maps or suit-mobility measurements.

What makes it creative

  • One decision, not a gallery. MOMAR combines data from many missions into a single route choice instead of showing separate maps side by side.
  • It shows the cost of safety: how much longer the lower-risk route is, and exactly what it avoids.
  • It turns spectral data into science stops along the route.
  • You can walk the plan in 3D before anyone walks it for real.
  • The same planner works on two worlds, Mars and the Moon.

Tools used: TypeScript, React 19, Next.js 16, Leaflet, Three.js, Tailwind CSS and Vitest; Python with rasterio/GDAL, NumPy, Shapely and spiceypy. It’s hosted as a static site, with one small server function for the optional AI assistant.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: no invented data, and archived data is never shown as live.
  • The limits of 20 m orbital terrain: boulders are too small to resolve at this scale, and the app says so.
  • Walking models built on Earth are not spacesuit data, so a second, gravity-scaled model is shown next to the first.
  • Accessibility and performance: reduced-motion support, layouts for phones, and graceful fallbacks when WebGL or an online data service isn’t available.
  • Licences are recorded for every dataset and 3D model.
